title: Module 2 · Lesson 5 — Testing and debugging non-deterministic systems

lines: Picture a vet clinic's booking agent at its launch demo.
The developer runs it once, the right appointment appears, and everyone applauds.
A week later, one booking in three lands on the wrong day.
The same request, sent twice, takes two different paths.
Normal tests assume the same input gives the same output.
Agents break that assumption, so the testing pyramid changes shape.
At the base, unit tests check tools, parsers, validators, and routing, with no model at all.
Above them, component tests replay recorded model responses, so they stay fast and repeatable.
Next, a small integration set runs the real model, with tolerant assertions.
At the top, statistical evaluation scores a golden dataset and gates releases.
Push as much logic as you can down the pyramid.
Save the expensive layer for what truly depends on model judgement.
Never assert exact output text, because a harmless prompt tweak will break it.
Assert on properties: the right tool, valid arguments, a cited source, and staying within budget.
Then run each case several times.
Hard rules must hold on every run, and the success rate must clear a threshold.
pass@k asks whether at least one of k runs succeeded: a capability measure.
pass^k asks whether all k succeeded: a reliability measure.

say.0: Pass at K asks whether at least one of K runs succeeded: a capability measure.
say.1: Pass hat K asks whether all K succeeded: a reliability measure.

lines: The clinic's demo was a pass@k result.
Production agents are judged on pass^k, which would have caught the problem before launch.

say.0: The clinic's demo was a pass at K result.
say.1: Production agents are judged on pass hat K, which would have caught the problem before launch.

lines: When an answer is wrong, the trace shows which stage failed, and each stage has its own fix.
A wrong tool calls for sharper descriptions, and wrong arguments call for a tighter schema.
The clinic's trace showed the right call returning a bad result, from a calendar tool with the wrong time zone.
So the fix belonged in the tool, not the prompt.
Your golden set needs the cases that break things, not just the happy path.
Add ambiguous requests, injected instructions, timeouts, and questions with no answer.
Exam tip: never assert exact strings, and judge production agents on pass^k, not pass@k.
Read on to build the pyramid, layer by layer.

say.0: Exam tip: never assert exact strings, and judge production agents on pass hat K, not pass at K.
